rows.description: A teenager who said something awkward at a party replays it for days and imagines everyone still thinking of it; repetition feels like problem solving but deepens the sting.
A student who failed a paper asks over and over why it happened and what it says about them without arriving at any plan; thinking about causes without action keeps the mood low.

A school-age child sees a classmate narrow the eyes and reads suspicion or anger, though the person may be squinting at a bright board. Checking the context, such as light and vision, avoids unfair conclusions.
A teenager with heavy, half-closed eyes after late screen time may look bored or rude in class, but is often simply tired. Adults can ask about sleep before assuming disrespect.

A parent sees a teenager absorbed for hours and cannot tell whether it is flow or compulsion. The difference shows afterward: flow leaves a person energised and having grown, while capture leaves them drained and restless.
A coworker sees a teammate gone silent and intense at their desk and waits before interrupting. Recognising flow in others and holding non-urgent questions is a quiet form of respect.

A child with a fracture or bad fall may be scared, angry at being stopped from playing and worried about the future. Comfort, honest information and small achievable goals help the mind heal along with the body.
A young adult in recovery feels impatient, dependent on others and annoyed at the slow pace, and may swing between overdoing and giving up. Steady, measured progress is better than either extreme.

A person after a road accident or serious injury may feel jumpy, avoid the place or vehicle and replay the event. Time, support and, if fear lingers, professional help allow trust in the world to return.
A toddler squeezes the eyes shut when scared, tired or refusing to look, and blinks slowly when sleepy. These are protective or tired signals, not defiance.
A preschooler finds winking hard and may blink both eyes, while a wink tells a friend about a joke or secret. Winking is playful, and its meaning depends on the shared understanding.

rows.subtype: Widening the eyes as a listening cue [Expressing]
rows.description: A young professional widens the eyes slightly to show interest and encourage a speaker. It works when natural, and a fixed wide-eyed look may seem strained.
A child with a homemade tiffin, a regional accent or older clothes is laughed at. They may shrink, copy the group or quietly resent it, learning early that difference carries a price.
A teenager is told that skipping class, vaping or a prank is what everyone does, with a hint of exclusion if they refuse. The threat is social, so it feels bigger than the act itself.
